title: CaseMaster: Designing and Evaluating a Probe for Oral Case Presentation Training with LLM Assistance
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI ’26)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of training medical students to deliver effective oral case presentations (OCPs), a core communication skill in clinical education. The authors argue that traditional OCP training methods—such as case discussion, case writing, and role-play—can be difficult to scale, may not provide enough structured guidance, and often fail to deliver timely, constructive feedback. They also identify an opportunity for large language models (LLMs) to support training, but note concerns about prompt burden, reliability, and integration into educational workflows.

To explore this space, the authors conducted a formative study with six medical educators to understand current OCP teaching practices, difficulties in student presentations, and attitudes toward LLM use. Based on these insights, they designed CaseMaster, a web-based system probe that supports OCP training through two stages: preparation and reflection. In preparation, students browse patient cases, draft presentations using the SOAP structure, and use preset LLM-assisted actions to search for key knowledge, evaluate logic, generate examples, and receive presentation advice. In reflection, they compare their responses against reference answers and receive rubric-based scoring and feedback generated with an LLM.

The evaluation involved two user studies in a hospital-linked medical education context in China. The first study compared CaseMaster with a baseline workflow among 12 university medical students completing OCP tasks; the second collected feedback from five experienced educators. Results suggested that CaseMaster improved presentation quality, confidence, and efficiency relative to the baseline workflow, while educators generally viewed the tool favorably but emphasized the need for careful use and critical review of LLM outputs. The paper concludes with design guidelines for creating adaptive, transparent, and user-centered LLM-based training tools for medical education.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed design-and-evaluation study with formative qualitative work plus a small controlled user study, but it is not a well-powered randomized trial and reports limited quantitative outcome evidence. The methodology is credible for prototype evaluation, yet the evidence base is mainly qualitative and early-stage.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests promising positive effects on presentation quality, confidence, and workload, but the impacts are not quantified with effect sizes and come from a small n=12 study. That makes the likely impact plausible but still modest and unclear for broader educational settings.

interventions.use_case: LLM-assisted oral case presentation training probe that generates case-specific content, suggests presentation improvements, searches key knowledge points, and provides reflective feedback/scoring on student presentations.
LLM-based validation and rubric scoring of student oral case presentations, highlighting omissions, discrepancies, and rubric-based performance across history, labs, assessment, plan, and style.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports that CaseMaster had the potential to improve presentation quality in oral case presentation training, with students and educators describing clearer, more coherent delivery. In the 12-student experiment, the authors state that the tool had positive impacts on confidence and presentation skills, but they do not report a standardized effect size for this outcome.
finding.measure: Oral case presentation quality / presentation skills, participant feedback on confidence and usability

finding.finding_summary: CaseMaster was designed to support structured reasoning, self-reflection, and error detection during case preparation and review. The paper reports that the reflection stage highlighted discrepancies and missing elements in student drafts, suggesting improved metacognitive review, but no quantitative effect size is provided for these learning-process outcomes.
finding.measure: Self-reflection, error identification, and structured reasoning during OCP preparation and review

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that CaseMaster can reduce workload compared with traditional methods by automating feedback and scoring, and educators reinforced this implication in qualitative feedback. However, the paper does not provide a quantified workload reduction estimate or time-on-task effect size.
finding.measure: Perceived workload / efficiency of feedback and evaluation workflow
finding.study_size: n=12 students; 5 educators in follow-up evaluation
